title: 400,000 Students Applied to Recheck Their CBSE Scores. IIT Roorkee Blinked. The Supreme Court Is Next.
excerpt: The fallout from CBSE's botched digital evaluation keeps widening. IIT Roorkee has waived its 75% eligibility cutoff. A student in Saudi Arabia received a blank marksheet. The Supreme Court hears the case today.
body:
When the Central Board of Secondary Education declared its Class 12 results on May 13, the pass rate was 85.2 percent — a drop of 3.19 percentage points from the previous year and the lowest in seven years. Out of 17.69 lakh students who appeared, 1.63 lakh were placed in the compartment category, meaning they must sit supplementary exams in July.

That was the first tremor. What followed has been an earthquake.

## The Scale of the Crisis

The numbers tell the story in full. Over 400,000 students — more than four lakh — have applied for rechecking of their scanned answer sheets. The Ministry of Education confirmed that by June 4, CBSE had received over 70,000 formal requests for post-result services, including 7,314 applications for verification of marks and 63,119 applications for re-evaluation. The number has since surged as the revaluation portal deadline was extended to midnight on June 7.

Students flagged mismatched answer sheets — pages in handwriting that wasn't theirs. Others reported missing pages, omitted supplementary sheets, and blurred scans. A student based in Saudi Arabia received a blank marksheet — no individual subject marks at all. That case has now reached the Supreme Court, which hears the matter today, June 8.

At the centre of the crisis is CBSE's decision to introduce On-Screen Marking for Class 12 evaluations for the first time in 2026. Under OSM, physical answer sheets are scanned and evaluated digitally by examiners working on screens. The system was contracted to Coempt Eduteck — a company that, as 17-year-old student Sarthak Sidhant exposed last month, was previously known as Globarena and was involved in the 2019 Telangana intermediate results controversy, where evaluation errors led to over 3.8 lakh students failing and 21 suicides.

## IIT Roorkee Bends the Rules

The ripple effects have reached India's most prestigious technical institutions. IIT Roorkee, which administers JEE Advanced counselling, has waived its standard requirement that CBSE students score at least 75 percent in their Class 12 board exams to be eligible for IIT admission.

The decision came after sustained pressure from students across social media platforms. On June 4, IIT Roorkee initially denied any relaxation. Within days, it reversed course. Under the new policy, candidates' participation in the admission process is contingent upon submitting a revised scorecard by July 15 — an implicit acknowledgment that the current CBSE scores may not be reliable.

The relaxation applies only to CBSE students. Since candidates from 36 different boards appeared for JEE, IIT Roorkee was initially reluctant to make changes for one board. But the scale of the CBSE crisis — and the political noise around it — forced its hand.

## The Political Dimension

The CBSE controversy has become a political flashpoint. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi met with Sarthak Sidhant, the student who exposed the CBSE-Coempt connection, and praised his work. "Mr. Modi wants our youth to keep making reels, keep frying pakoras, not ask questions," Gandhi said on X. "But these kids asked questions. And they found the answers too."

Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh demanded the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, accusing his ministry of "incompetence" in overseeing the OSM rollout. "CBSE has now stopped using Coempt's platform and built its own website for the re-evaluation process," Ramesh said, calling it a "final admission that COEMPT's portal was irretrievably compromised."

The Cabinet Secretariat has constituted a one-member committee to examine the procurement process behind the OSM system.

## The Cybersecurity Dimension

The technical failures go beyond evaluation errors. Nineteen-year-old ethical hacker Nisarga Adhikary, a CBSE Class 12 student himself, claimed he found serious security flaws in the OSM portal and reported them to the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) in February 2026. Most remained unfixed. Adhikary alleged that examiners' accounts could be accessed using publicly available details and a password exposed in the system's source code. He further claimed that answer sheets and question papers stored on an Amazon Web Services server were publicly accessible due to improper configuration.

CBSE's post-result services portal faced 1.5 million hits in two minutes when it launched, effectively crashing the system and leaving students unable to apply for rechecking.

## What Comes Next

The Supreme Court hearing on June 8 could be pivotal. If the court orders a broader audit of the OSM system — or mandates re-evaluation for students who allege discrepancies — the downstream effects on JEE Advanced, medical entrance exams, and university admissions could cascade through the entire academic calendar.

For the 17.69 lakh students who sat for CBSE Class 12 in 2026, the crisis is not abstract. It is about college admissions, scholarship eligibility, and the professional programmes that determine the trajectory of their lives. The board's decision to digitise evaluation was meant to reduce manual errors. Instead, it has produced the most severe crisis of institutional trust in Indian education in a decade — and the consequences are still unfolding.
